Construction of access roads, tunnel portals, and the tie station (the latter area already discussed) would permanently remove 95 acres of wildlife habitats.
Approximately 315 acres of land would be altered in varying degrees through establishment of the Bad Creek to Oconee and Bad Creek to Jocassee transmission line rightsof-way. Vegetation along the transmission line rights-ofway would be selectively cleared to the extent possible and periodically maintained to assure safe permanent line clearances. Construction access would be from existing logging roads where possible with some additional temporary road construction where needed. Diversification of existing wildlife habitats would result from limited localized clearing around transmission line towers and periodic selective cutting for maintenance of the right-of-way. Early plant succession favorable to ruffed grouse would be perpetuated. Deer, cottontail, bobwhite quail, and other species would benefit from woodland openings. Turkey could also benefit from small clearings. In contrast, wildlife adapted to mature forest habitats would be expected to decrease locally.
3.1.2.3 Water Quality and Aquatic Fauna
The major impacts of construction would be increases in sediments and turbidity caused by runoff from land clearing and construction of project works. Bad Creek, West Bad Creek, and Howard Creek already show the effects of siltation as a result of road construction, logging activities, and preliminary exploration associated with the Bad Creek Project. Sediments and increased turbidity have occurred as a result of these activities, and many sections of streambed are now covered by layers of silt that provide a much poorer habitat for aquatic organisms than gravel and cobble bottom.
Erosion could be especially acute in the upper reservoir area since the site would be cleared to bare ground. Soils in the Bad Creek - West Bad Creek area are subject to severe erosion. Howard Creek from South Carolina Highway 171 to Lake Jocassee (about 3.5 miles of stream) would be the major stream affected outside the upper reservoir.
